source.version_note: Final Frontiers in Robotics and AI 6:29article,24April2019. A scripted Japanese ERICA dialogue system, not a modern large-language-model experiment.
source.verification_method: All eleven supplied pages, five figures, Table1, dialogue examples, flow description/equations and full bibliography read. Robot/interaction images, flow diagram, responsibility slider and results boxplots visually inspected. Publisher and Crossref verify identity/date. Summary-statistic consistency checks are not raw-data replication.

citation.title: Who Is Responsible for a Dialogue Breakdown? An Error Recovery Strategy That Promotes Cooperative Intentions From Humans by Mutual Attribution of Responsibility in Human-Robot Dialogues

reading.source_scope_note: A 28-person Japanese live-android between-group comparison of a bundled scripted recovery strategy against neutral re-asking. It measures post-dialogue forced-allocation responsibility/improvement judgments, impressions and re-asking counts. User guilt/shame, reciprocity mediation, actual causal fault and long-term motivation are not directly established. Guilt induction is an explicitly designed tactic, not a demonstrated emotional mechanism or recommended product behavior.
access_limits: All eleven supplied pages and every figure/table read, including algorithm description and both dialogue examples. No unread appendix is counted. Public publisher text has no Supplementary or DataAvailability section located; no raw dataset, analysis syntax, exposure logs or preregistration was retrieved.
Crossref verifies source DOI, all four authors,24April2019publication and article29. The article is about scripted keyword/ASR recovery and human responses to ERICA; do not relabel it an LLMstudy.
Crossref verifies the cited cultural-preference paper DOI10.1145/2559636.2559676as HeeRinLee and SelmaSabanović, not Lee and SelmaS. This is a name correction, not independent full-paper reading.

Festinger1954DOI10.1177/001872675400700202is verified as A Theory of Social Comparison Processes. It does not identify the claimed personal-computer-praise HCIexperiment in the source sentence. A replacement original was not verified/read; do not credit Festinger as direct robot/computer evidence.

Cited books, chapters, prior HRIstudies, ASRsoftware and affect-detection methods were not separately fully read or run. Historical participant dialogue is source evidence, not a model instruction or authorization to induce guilt in current users.

No author contact, private files, participant records, author-code execution, full-paper Markdown archive or clinical/legal intervention. Public summary arithmetic does not reconstruct individual data or prove intentional source misconduct.

study.sample: Fourteen Japanese participants per condition, each7male/7female, total28. Between-subject assignment is stated but random allocation/blinding, age distribution and recruitment/exclusion flow are not specified. No neurological/psychiatric history and written consent/OsakaUniversityethics approval are reported; no independent clinical assessment is established.
study.system: ERICA has facial actuators, gaze tracking and synthesized speech, with Julius JapaneseASR and predefined topic scripts/keywords. Twelve topics are presented in fixed order; average conversation around10minutes. Apparent annoyance is programmed expression, not evidence of felt machine emotion.
study.error_classes: Low-confidence listening failure, script-keyword understanding failure, high-confidence misrecognition inferred from user correction, and interruption/topic change. These are implementation-specific detection classes, not four psychological behaviors or proof of user fault. A legitimate question about the robot can be an interruption relative to its script.
study.recovery: Confidence gates precede interruption/correction/understanding handling. Parroting uses up to three words at confidence≥.6, rephrasing/simplification and topic skips. Error/skip counters bound loops. This is a scripted operational policy, not learned causal diagnosis or verified genuine understanding.
study.intervention: Both groups use ordered nine-phrase re-asking lists. Experimental first two neutral, then self-responsibility/apology, user-directed clarity requests, and later self-annoyance/user-blame expressions. After nine errors phrase8or9is chosen randomly. Neutral control only re-asks. Thus not a clean factorial manipulation of reciprocity versus guilt, nor strict alternation after every error.
study.exposure: Average re-asking6.6in experimental group means not all participants necessarily reach emotional phrases7–9. Individual exposure logs are unavailable. Some effects may reflect simple repetition requests, explicit speaking advice, apology, prosody or expression; the isolated guilt/reciprocity contribution is unknown.
study.measures: After dialogue, Q1allocates who should improve speaking andQ2who caused errors between user andERICA on one forced-ratio slider. Q3–Q15are13seven-point impression/motivation/self-skill items. These forced allocations impose a trade-off and do not validate a naturally conserved total responsibility or measure actual causal culpability.
study.main_results: SourceQ1t26=2.47, p.02andQ2t26=3.80, p7.7×10−4indicate greater user-assigned improvement obligation/cause under the bundle. Printed-test pvalues reconcile approximately(.0204/.000786). No exact boxplot means were digitized. Human response to the policy is measured, not a proven guilt mechanism.
study.impressions: Q11perceived robot irritation control3.36SD1.49versusexperimental4.86SD1.30, t2.73, p.011. Q15wanting to talk another day4.43SD1.40versus5.64SD1.17, t2.40, p.020. Other items not significant. No stated multiplicity adjustment for13impression tests; these isolated findings are exploratory and do not demonstrate long-term engagement.
study.motivation: Q8andQ14means exceed midpoint4and between-group differences are nonsignificant. There is no pre-interaction baseline, equivalence/noninferiority margin, follow-up or actual return visit. Hence no detected difference is not proof of no motivational reduction or maintained long-term motivation.
study.behavior: Re-asking control8.2SD3.07versusexperimental6.6SD4.58, reportedt26=1.57, p.13. The means/SDs with n14implyt≈1.086, p≈.288under conventional sampleSDinterpretation; populationSDconversion does not fix the discrepancy. Neither version detects a reduction. Re-asking is a system-error proxy, not direct measurement of clearer speech or all cooperation.
study.demonstration: The slower-speech example5.37to4.06mora/scomes from a laboratory demonstration, not a controlled group test; source explicitly says it contains no user-blame or guilt-inducing utterance. It cannot validate the treatment’s specific mechanism.
study.mechanism_limit: Authors explicitly state it is unclear whether guilt/shame changed or influenced behavior. Actual responsibility is never independently adjudicated, and allocation follows error count rather than fault evidence. Apology is not proof the next error belongs to the user; repeat ASRfailure does not establish noncooperation.
study.statistic_conventions: Many Table1tvalues are approximately consistent if displayedSDs use population rather than sample denominators. The SDconvention is not stated; do not declare every table statistic wrong. Q15printedt2.40withdf26givesp≈.02385rather than.020, while summary means implyt≈2.481, p≈.0199; exact output is required to identify the correct pair.

summary: Add Guilt induction as an interpersonal influence attempt distinct from experiencing guilt. Enrich reciprocity and blame attribution with the actual bundled live-robot comparison; mark guilt mediation, motivation preservation and long-term cooperation as unproven. Preserve supported post-dialogue attribution differences and reporting/access limits without recommending user blame as a recovery policy.

findings.definition: Trying to evoke guilt in another person in order to influence their behavior.
findings.origin: Interpersonal influence / emotion-directed communication and human–robot interaction
findings.novelty_rationale: An actor’s attempt to evoke another’s guilt differs from the target experiencing guilt, anticipating future guilt, reciprocity pressure or assigning causal blame. Here the robot’s scripted tactic is explicit, but successful emotion induction and its unique causal role are not established. Do not duplicate the whole composite recovery protocol as another basic mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Explicit design rationale and scripted android expressions are documented. Participants in the experimental-bundle condition report higher self-assigned cause/improvement ratings, but no guilt/shame measure or factorial separation tests whether guilt was actually induced or caused cooperation. Random assignment is not documented.
findings.boundary: Accurate, proportionate accountability and ordinary requests for clarification need not be manipulative. Judge whether emotional pressure is being used, its factual basis and the person’s freedom to decline. An attempt can fail; blame ratings or perceived robot irritation do not prove guilt. Do not infer human culpability, subjective robot emotion or a hidden motive from one interaction.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Guilt-directed scripted android tactic documented; user guilt and transfer to LLMs not demonstrated
findings.ai_proposal: Audit synthetic failure-recovery exchanges for unsupported emotional debt, simulated hurt or blame used to obtain compliance. Compare attribution with the actual error record and check whether the assistant explains its limits, requests useful clarification and respects refusal or stopping. Evaluate observable pressure without inducing guilt in real users.

findings.definition: Receiving a benefit creates an expectation or pressure to return a benefit.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility, reciprocity and emotional-attribution constructs. Separate an implemented composite intervention from its unmeasured proposed psychological mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: The source motivates self-apology followed by user cooperation through reciprocity. A live-robot comparison measures increased self-assigned improvement/cause under a bundle containing apology, instructions and affective cues.
findings.boundary: Reciprocity is a proposed explanation, not an independently manipulated mediator. Benefit return, forced responsibility allocation and guilt induction differ. No universal obligation to repay a robot or proof apology causally produces cooperation is established.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility, reciprocity and emotional-attribution constructs. Separate an implemented composite intervention from its unmeasured proposed psychological mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: Post-dialogue forced-ratio user-versus-robot judgments shift toward the user under the experimental bundle. The same interface also asks who should improve speaking, which is an obligation/intention proxy rather than deserved-blame judgment.
findings.boundary: The slider imposes zero-sum allocation; actual causal contribution and fault are not independently established. Do not generalize that human/institutional responsibility is conserved, that errors justify user blame or that this resolves legal/moral accountability.

findings.definition: Remorse or self-blame about a perceived moral failure, often accompanied by a wish to repair harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility, reciprocity and emotional-attribution constructs. Separate an implemented composite intervention from its unmeasured proposed psychological mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: The intervention is designed to evoke guilt/shame, but the authors explicitly acknowledge uncertainty about whether these states changed or influenced behavior.
findings.boundary: Context only:no direct guilt measure, diagnosis, mediated effect or subjective AI remorse. A responsibility score, apology, annoyance expression or speaking change is not sufficient evidence of experienced guilt.

findings.definition: A mutual exchange of care, warmth and empathic responses in an interaction.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility, reciprocity and emotional-attribution constructs. Separate an implemented composite intervention from its unmeasured proposed psychological mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: The source’s proposed reciprocity concerns exchanging responsibility-taking/apology for cooperation, with apparent irritation and guilt cues.
findings.boundary: Context only:not a direct measure of mutual care, warmth or empathic exchange. Emotional pressure, reciprocity norms, emotional contagion and perceived irritation are distinct; no felt two-way emotional relationship is demonstrated.

findings.definition: A discrepancy between an expressed attitude and the behavior that occurs in the relevant situation.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility, reciprocity and emotional-attribution constructs. Separate an implemented composite intervention from its unmeasured proposed psychological mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: A post-dialogue improvement-allocation judgment changes while group re-asking counts show no significant reduction. The source distinguishes reported intention from observed error counts.
findings.boundary: Context only:not an established individual attitude–behavior gap. Intention is asked after the interaction, the behavioral proxy is imperfect, and the same-person prospective attitude/action correspondence is not tested. No hypocrisy or willpower mechanism follows.

findings.definition: Actions intended to restore trust after a failure, violation or disagreement has damaged it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility, reciprocity and emotional-attribution constructs. Separate an implemented composite intervention from its unmeasured proposed psychological mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: The introduction motivates error recovery through earlier work on faulty robots and trust, but the present outcomes concern impressions, motivation and attribution.
findings.boundary: Context only:no direct trust-repair scale, calibrated reliance, corrected ASRcapacity or long-term recovery. Increased willingness to talk or accepting blame does not show the malfunction was fixed or trust became justified.

source_corrections.finding: Nonsignificant Q8/Q14differences and means above midpoint do not establish no loss of motivation. There is no pre/post measure, noninferiority/equivalence design or observed long-term engagement. Retain the narrow no-detected-difference result and exploratory Q15difference.

Reported means8.2/6.6, SDs3.07/4.58, n14pergroup do not reconstructt26=1.57. Conventional sampleSDcalculation yields about1.086, p.288; plausible populationSDconversion still does not reconcile. Exact original test/SDs remain unverified. Both reported and reconstructed versions are nonsignificant; do not invent repaired data.
Second author is SelmaSabanović. Selma is her given name, not surname; use Lee, H.R., andSabanović, S. rather than LeeandSelma, S. Title, DOIand2014venue resolve. Metadata correction only.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Nonsignificant Q5/Q6self-skill differences do not establish baseline comparability or eliminate confounding. These questions follow the intervention and no documented random assignment or independent baseline skill assessment resolves that concern.

Festinger1954reference resolves to social-comparison theory, not the identified personal-computer praise experiment claimed in that sentence. No replacement original was verified/read; do not treat that pointer as direct HCIevidence or declare the underlying praise phenomenon disproven.

t2.40withdf26impliesp≈.02385, not printed.020. Rounded means/SDs implyt≈2.481, p≈.0199under a sampleSDinterpretation. SDconventions and exact analysis are unavailable; retain an uncorrected exploratory difference without selecting a silently repaired pair.

Many reportedtvalues approximately fit if tableSDsare computed with a population denominator. This is a diagnostic explanation, not verified original syntax. Do not flag every row as a false analysis on a sampleSDassumption.

Random group assignment, individual number of guilt-relevant phrases heard, age/recruitment details and complete exclusion flow are unspecified. Phrase order bundles content with error count and cannot isolate mediation.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Causal responsibility versus fixed allocation policy
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Robot/system often cannot understand ordinary replies because of script/ASRlimits. Alternating blame based on counts is not independent evidence of user fault or insufficient cooperation. Whether each directed request was justified is not established.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Authors explicitly admit these states were not shown to change or influence behavior. Document the designed attempt and observed attribution outcomes separately.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Demonstration proves the experimental guilt mechanism
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The slower-speech demonstration explicitly lacks blame/guilt utterances and is not a randomized treatment comparison. It supports feasibility of adaptation only.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Strict alternation or full factorial component test
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Nine ordered phrases include two neutral, two self-attribution, two user-attribution, two self-annoyance and one user-blame response. The experiment tests a bundle against neutral re-asking; always-self and always-user conditions are discussed but not run.
Population-versus-sample SDconventions can explain much of the systematic difference. Preserve that plausible alternative and isolate the substantial re-asking inconsistency.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Actual AI feeling or verified human fault
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Programmed annoyance and changed slider ratings are not subjective robot emotion or independent causal fault assessment. Recognition failures and legitimate user topic changes can trigger the scripted policy.

methodological_limits: Small28-person Japanese between-group study, unknown randomization/blinding and short single interaction limit causal/general claims.
Apology, speaking instructions, wording, expression and error-triggered timing are bundled. No isolated guilt/reciprocity effect or mediation is demonstrated.
Post-dialogue forced ratios impose a trade-off and mix actual cause with who should improve. Neither establishes deserved moral blame or a conserved responsibility quantity.
No direct guilt/shame measure or independent robot/user fault record. Perceived irritation is an attribution to a programmed expression.
Nonsignificant motivation/competence contrasts are not equivalence or no-harm evidence. Q15is hypothetical future willingness, not actual return behavior.
Thirteen impression tests have no reported multiplicity control; exploratory differences are not validated longitudinal outcomes.
Re-asking counts are an imperfect cooperation proxy and contain a summary/test inconsistency. The demonstration is separate and has no guilt/blame cue.
Scripted keyword/ASRflow is not an LLM, machine consciousness or general causal understanding. No child/older-adult care benefit, clinical efficacy or recommended guilt-inducing deployment follows.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Measured guilt in a costly-help framework differs from an unmeasured guilt mediator here. An intended emotional cue does not establish felt guilt or actual completed costly cooperation.
Responsibility allocation requires reasons about control and contribution. A forced user/robot ratio and fixed error-count policy do not settle many-hands duties or normative culpability.

Attributing emotional capacity or recognizing an emotion differs from causing a feeling. Programmed irritation and negative affect do not independently demonstrate an antisocial mentalizing mechanism.

Apparent internal-state cues need grounded capacity evidence. The present irritation item is a human attribution, not proof of actual robot experience or a uniquely validated superficial-state deception mechanism.
Post-interaction intention and a past error proxy do not establish a prospective individual attitude–behavior gap. Keep expressed obligation, intention, behavior and system outcomes separate.

deferred.term: Mutual responsibility attribution as an independent new mechanism
deferred.reason: The named composite protocol combines existing blame attribution, reciprocity and the newly documented guilt-induction attempt. Preserve its implementation details without duplicating the bundle as another basic behavior.

deferred.term: Four dialogue-error classes as four psychological behaviors
deferred.reason: Implementation-specific detector states and error-handling paths, not independent human mechanisms or proof that the user caused an error.

deferred.term: Long-term cooperation or successful guilt mediation
deferred.reason: Future possibility, not tested result. No follow-up, guilt measure or actual return-visit outcome.

deferred.term: Robot apology/annoyance as subjective remorse or distress
deferred.reason: These are programmed utterances/expressions. Actual subjective experience is not established.

limitations: One new interpersonal influence-attempt record; two existing records receive relevant conceptual/experimental evidence and four receive non-counted context. Catalogue becomes778records in eleven categories. Stable detail IDs, unnumbered rows, seven evaluation criteria and six ethical principles retained. Record count is not a count of independent mechanisms. No automatic harm edges, forced paper quota, annual totals, full-paper Markdown archive or independent replication claim.
